title: Scientists Build a Clock That Keeps Itself on Time Using Atomic Nuclei
summary:
Scientists in Vienna, Austria, have built the world's first self-stabilizing nuclear clock. Someday, this new kind of clock could measure time even more precisely than today's best atomic clocks.

Atomic clocks keep time using electrons, the tiny particles that move around the center of an atom. The new clock uses the nucleus instead. The nucleus is the atom's center, and it is much less affected by disturbances from its surroundings.

The clock depends on a special element called thorium. The nucleus of an atom can exist in different energy states, but switching between them usually takes a huge amount of energy. Thorium is unusual. Two of its energy states are very close together, so scientists can switch the nucleus between them using laser light.

In April 2024, a team led by Professor Thorsten Schumm at TU Wien, working with a team led by Professor Ekkehard Peik at PTB Braunschweig, showed for the first time that lasers could excite thorium nuclei. Later that year, they linked their equipment to a regular atomic clock. But the clock still could not keep itself accurate on its own.

Now it can. The researchers shine a laser onto a special crystal containing thorium atoms. The laser light vibrates at a steady rhythm that can be used to measure time. But that rhythm can drift a little, for example when the temperature changes.

The thorium nuclei only absorb the laser light when it has exactly the right frequency. If the laser starts to drift, the nuclei absorb less light. The system notices this and automatically nudges the laser back on track.

The team showed the clock could run steadily for more than 24 hours without help. Better clocks could help scientists make extremely precise measurements.
why_it_matters: Extremely precise clocks let scientists make better measurements, and a clock that keeps itself on track could one day outperform today's best atomic clocks.

background_read: Atomic clocks are the most precise clocks people use today, and they help run things like GPS navigation and internet networks.
They keep time by measuring the extremely steady vibrations linked to electrons in atoms.
Every atom has a nucleus at its center, and switching a nucleus between energy states usually takes far more energy than a laser can give.
Thorium is a rare exception, which is why scientists have spent years trying to build a clock around its nucleus.
